ACECLOFENAC.uses: A pain and anti-inflammatory medicine used for joint pain, back pain, and swelling after injury.
how: Usually taken twice a day after food
Swallow whole with water, don't crush unless told to
avoid: Long-term use without a doctor's advice
Use in pregnancy, especially the third trimester, without medical advice
forms: Tablet (oral) — for joint/back pain and general inflammation
Topical gel — applied directly over the painful joint/muscle, e.g. Hifenac-P Gel

ACETAZOLAMIDE.uses: Reduces fluid pressure inside the eye (glaucoma) and is also used to prevent altitude sickness.
how: Taken as directed, often 1–4 times a day
Take with food to reduce stomach upset
sideEffects: Tingling in hands, feet, or lips
avoid: Driving if you feel drowsy or tingly
forms: Tablet (oral) — glaucoma, altitude sickness (most common household form)
Injection (IV) — hospital use only, for acute glaucoma or fluid overload

ACETYLSALICYLIC ACID.uses: Also called Aspirin. Used in low doses to prevent heart attacks and strokes, and in higher doses for pain and fever.
how: Low-dose tablets are usually taken once daily
Take with or after food to protect the stomach
avoid: Giving to children under 16 (risk of Reye's syndrome)
Combining with other painkillers without advice

ALBENDAZOLE.uses: An antiparasitic medicine used to treat worm infections in the intestine.
how: Usually taken as a single dose or short course
Chew or crush the tablet and take with a meal
seeDoctor: Fever, sore throat, or unusual bruising/bleeding (rare blood-count effects, especially with repeated courses)
avoid: Use during pregnancy without medical advice

ALLOPURINOL.uses: Lowers uric acid levels in the blood to prevent gout attacks and kidney stones.
how: Taken once daily after food
Drink plenty of water while on this medicine
avoid: Stopping suddenly during a gout flare without advice
forms: Tablet (oral) — long-term gout prevention (most common household form)
Injection (IV) — hospital use only, e.g. during chemotherapy

AMITRIPTYLINE.uses: Used in low doses for nerve pain and to help prevent migraines; in higher doses it treats depression.
how: Usually taken once at night since it can cause drowsiness
Effects for pain may take 1–2 weeks to show
avoid: Driving until you know how it affects you

AMLODIPINE.uses: A blood pressure medicine that relaxes blood vessels, also used for chest pain (angina).
how: Taken once daily, with or without food
Take at the same time each day

AMOXICILLIN.uses: An antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections of the ear, throat, chest, urine and skin.
how: Usually taken 2–3 times a day, spaced evenly
Can be taken with or without food
avoid: Stopping early even if you feel better
forms: Capsule/Tablet/Syrup (oral) — most common household form
Injection (IV) — hospital use only, for more serious infections

AMOXICILLIN + CLAVULANIC ACID.uses: A stronger antibiotic combination used for infections that plain amoxicillin can't fully treat.
how: Usually taken 2–3 times a day with food to reduce stomach upset
Complete the full course
forms: Tablet/Syrup (oral) — most common household form
Injection (IV) — hospital use only

ATORVASTATIN.uses: A cholesterol-lowering medicine that reduces the risk of heart attack and stroke.
how: Usually taken once daily, often at night
Can be taken with or without food
seeDoctor: Unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness

AZITHROMYCIN.uses: An antibiotic used for respiratory, skin, and some sexually transmitted infections.
how: Usually taken once daily for 3–5 days
Take on an empty stomach unless told otherwise

BACLOFEN.uses: A muscle relaxant used for muscle spasms and stiffness, often from spinal or nerve conditions.
how: Usually started at a low dose and increased gradually
Take with food if it upsets your stomach
avoid: Driving until you know how it affects you

CARBAMAZEPINE.uses: Used to control seizures (epilepsy) and certain types of nerve pain, including trigeminal neuralgia.
how: Usually taken 2–3 times a day with food
Dose is often increased slowly by your doctor

CEFIXIME.uses: An antibiotic used for infections of the throat, ear, urinary tract, and chest.
how: Usually taken once or twice daily
Can be taken with or without food
seeDoctor: Confusion, convulsions, or unusual movements (rare, more likely with reduced kidney function)

CETIRIZINE.uses: An antihistamine used to relieve allergy symptoms like sneezing, runny nose, and itchy eyes.
how: Usually taken once daily, with or without food
Can be taken at night if it makes you drowsy
avoid: Driving if it makes you sleepy

CHLOROQUINE.uses: Used to prevent and treat malaria, and sometimes for certain autoimmune conditions.
how: Take exactly as prescribed for prevention or treatment
Take with food to reduce stomach upset
avoid: Skipping doses during a malaria prevention course
forms: Tablet/Syrup (oral) — malaria prevention/treatment at home
Injection — hospital use only, for severe malaria

CHOLECALCIFEROL.uses: Vitamin D3 — a fat-soluble vitamin the body needs to absorb calcium and keep bones, teeth, and muscles healthy. Used to treat or prevent vitamin D deficiency, and to support treatment of bone conditions like osteoporosis, rickets, and osteomalacia. Very commonly prescribed in India, since limited sun exposure, indoor lifestyles, and covered clothing mean deficiency is widespread even in a sunny country.
how: Taken as directed — daily, weekly, or monthly depending on the dose
Take with a meal containing some fat for better absorption
seeDoctor: Symptoms of too much vitamin D: nausea, vomiting, weakness, confusion (rare with correct dosing)
avoid: Taking much higher doses than prescribed
forms: Sachet/granules and capsules (oral) — most common household form, often a single high dose (e.g. 60,000 IU)
Injection (IM) — e.g. Arachitol, usually hospital/clinic-administered for severe deficiency

CIPROFLOXACIN.uses: A broad-spectrum antibiotic (fluoroquinolone) used for urinary tract, respiratory, and some gut and typhoid infections. Also formulated as eye or ear drops for bacterial eye/ear infections, and as an IV form for more serious infections treated in hospital. It works by blocking bacteria from copying their own DNA, so it has no effect on viral infections like a cold or flu.
how: Usually taken twice daily
Drink plenty of water; avoid dairy near dosing time
seeDoctor: Unusual mood or mental changes (confusion, agitation, or severe anxiety)
avoid: Dairy products and antacids near dosing time
Strenuous exercise if you notice tendon pain
forms: Tablet/capsule/syrup (oral) — for systemic infections, most common household form
Eye/ear drops — for bacterial conjunctivitis or ear infections, e.g. Ciplox Eye/Ear Drops
Injection (IV) — hospital use only, for more serious infections

CLARITHROMYCIN.uses: An antibiotic (macrolide) used for chest, throat, sinus, and skin infections. Also used as part of a combination treatment to clear H. pylori, the bacteria responsible for many stomach ulcers. Often prescribed as an alternative for people who are allergic to penicillin.
how: Usually taken twice daily
Can be taken with or without food

CLINDAMYCIN.uses: An antibiotic used for skin, dental, bone, and certain deep tissue infections, especially ones that don't respond well to more commonly used antibiotics. Available as an oral capsule for infections inside the body and as a topical gel or lotion for acne. Often chosen for people allergic to penicillin, or for infections involving bacteria that don't need oxygen to grow (anaerobic bacteria).
how: Usually taken 3–4 times a day with a full glass of water
Can be taken with food
seeDoctor: Severe or bloody diarrhoea (can happen even weeks after stopping)
avoid: Lying down immediately after taking it
forms: Capsule (oral) — for systemic infections
Topical gel/lotion — for acne, e.g. Clindac-A Gel
Injection (IV) — hospital use only, for serious infections

CLONAZEPAM.uses: A benzodiazepine used to control certain seizure disorders (including absence seizures) and to manage panic disorder or severe anxiety. It works by calming overactive electrical activity in the brain. Usually prescribed for short-term use, or carefully monitored long-term use, because of the risk of dependence.
how: Take exactly as prescribed, usually once or twice daily
Can be taken with or without food
avoid: Driving until you know how it affects you

CLOPIDOGREL.uses: A blood-thinning (antiplatelet) medicine that stops platelets from sticking together and forming clots. Used to prevent heart attacks and strokes, especially in people with a history of one, and is critical after a coronary stent to stop the stent from clotting shut. Often prescribed alongside low-dose aspirin for a set period after a stent procedure or heart attack.
how: Usually taken once daily
Take at the same time each day
avoid: Stopping suddenly without medical advice (risk of clot)
Taking with other blood thinners unless told to

CLOTRIMAZOLE.uses: An antifungal used for fungal skin infections (like ringworm and athlete's foot) and vaginal thrush. It comes as a cream or powder for the skin, a vaginal pessary/tablet or cream for thrush, and an oral 'mouth paint' or lozenge for oral thrush — the right form and application method depends on which one you have, so check the packaging.
how: Apply to the affected area as directed, usually 2–3 times daily
Wash and dry the area before applying
sideEffects: Mild burning or irritation at the site
avoid: Stopping treatment early even if symptoms improve
forms: Cream/powder — for skin fungal infections
Vaginal pessary/tablet or cream — for vaginal thrush, e.g. Candid-V
Oral mouth paint/lozenge — for oral thrush

DIAZEPAM.uses: A benzodiazepine used short-term for anxiety, muscle spasms, and to control seizures; also used to ease alcohol withdrawal symptoms and to calm patients before certain medical or dental procedures. It works by calming overactive nerve activity in the brain. In hospitals it's also given as an injection or rectal gel for emergency seizure control.
how: Take exactly as prescribed
Can be taken with or without food
avoid: Driving until you know how it affects you
forms: Tablet (oral) — most common household form
Injection/rectal gel — hospital or emergency use for active seizures

DICLOFENAC.uses: A pain and anti-inflammatory medicine for joint pain, muscle pain, and swelling.
how: Usually taken 2–3 times a day after food
Gel forms are applied directly to the painful area
seeDoctor: Swelling of face or difficulty breathing

DICYCLOMINE.uses: Used to relieve stomach cramps and spasms, including in irritable bowel syndrome.
how: Usually taken before meals, 3–4 times daily
Follow your doctor's dosing instructions
avoid: Driving if it blurs your vision or makes you drowsy

DIGOXIN.uses: A heart medicine used to treat certain irregular heart rhythms and heart failure.
how: Taken once daily at the same time
Do not double a missed dose
avoid: Taking extra doses even if you feel unwell

DILTIAZEM.uses: A blood pressure and heart rhythm medicine, also used for chest pain (angina).
how: Usually taken once or twice daily
Swallow extended-release tablets whole, don't crush

DOMPERIDONE.uses: Used to relieve nausea, vomiting, and bloating by helping the stomach empty faster.
how: Usually taken 15–30 minutes before meals, up to 3 times a day
Use for the shortest time needed
avoid: Use for longer than advised by your doctor
Combining with certain heart medicines without advice

DONEPEZIL.uses: Used to help with memory and thinking symptoms in Alzheimer's disease.
how: Usually taken once daily at bedtime
Can be taken with or without food

DOXYCYCLINE.uses: An antibiotic used for chest, skin, and some sexually transmitted infections, and for malaria prevention.
how: Usually taken once or twice daily with a full glass of water
Take with food to reduce stomach upset
seeDoctor: Severe skin burning after sun exposure
avoid: Lying down right after taking it
Dairy or antacids near dosing time

ENALAPRIL.uses: A blood pressure medicine (ACE inhibitor) also used in heart failure.
how: Usually taken once or twice daily
Can be taken with or without food
seeDoctor: Swelling of face, lips or throat
avoid: Salt substitutes high in potassium without checking with your doctor

ETODOLAC.uses: A pain and anti-inflammatory medicine used for arthritis, joint pain, and general pain relief.
how: Usually taken once or twice daily with food
Swallow whole, don't crush extended-release tablets
seeDoctor: Swelling of face or difficulty breathing

KETOROLAC.uses: A strong short-term pain reliever, often used after surgery or for severe acute pain.
how: Used only for short periods (usually up to 5 days)
Take with food to protect your stomach
seeDoctor: Swelling of face or difficulty breathing
avoid: Using for longer than your doctor advises
Combining with other NSAIDs like ibuprofen or diclofenac

METFORMIN.uses: A first-line medicine for type 2 diabetes that helps control blood sugar levels.
how: Usually taken with meals to reduce stomach upset
It can take a few weeks to see the full effect on blood sugar
seeDoctor: Unusual muscle pain along with weakness
avoid: Skipping meals right after a dose

OMEPRAZOLE.uses: Reduces stomach acid; used for acidity, reflux, and ulcers.
how: Usually taken once daily before breakfast
Swallow the capsule whole, don't chew

PANTOPRAZOLE.uses: Reduces stomach acid; used for acidity, reflux, and ulcers.
how: Usually taken once daily before a meal
Swallow the tablet whole, don't crush

LOSARTAN.uses: A blood pressure medicine (ARB) also used to protect the kidneys in diabetes.
how: Usually taken once daily
Can be taken with or without food
avoid: Salt substitutes high in potassium without checking with your doctor

IBUPROFEN.uses: A common pain, fever, and anti-inflammatory medicine used for headaches, muscle pain, and fever.
how: Usually taken every 6–8 hours with food
Do not exceed the maximum daily dose on the label
seeDoctor: Swelling of face or difficulty breathing
avoid: Long-term daily use without medical advice

AMBROXOL.uses: A cough medicine that helps loosen and clear mucus from the airways.
how: Usually taken 2-3 times a day
Can be taken with or without food
Drink plenty of water alongside it
avoid: Combining with other cough suppressants unless advised

AMIODARONE.uses: Used to control serious irregular heart rhythms.
how: Taken exactly as prescribed, often once daily
Take with food to reduce stomach upset

BISOPROLOL.uses: A beta-blocker used for high blood pressure, chest pain, and certain heart rhythm problems.
how: Taken once daily, usually in the morning
Can be taken with or without food

BUDESONIDE.uses: An inhaled steroid used to control asthma and prevent asthma attacks; also used as a nasal spray for allergies.
how: Used regularly as directed, even when you feel well
Rinse your mouth with water after using the inhaler
avoid: Skipping the mouth rinse after inhaler use

CANDESARTAN.uses: A blood pressure medicine (ARB) also used in some cases of heart failure.
how: Usually taken once daily
Can be taken with or without food
avoid: Salt substitutes high in potassium without checking with your doctor

CEFUROXIME.uses: An antibiotic used for respiratory, urinary, skin, and ENT infections.
how: Usually taken twice daily with food
Complete the full course
avoid: Relying solely on hormonal birth control pills during treatment — antibiotics can occasionally reduce how well they work

CHLORPHENIRAMINE.uses: An antihistamine used for allergy symptoms, hay fever, and itching.
how: Usually taken every 4-6 hours as needed
Can cause drowsiness, so caution when driving
avoid: Driving or operating machinery if drowsy

CILNIDIPINE.uses: A blood pressure medicine that relaxes blood vessels, commonly used for hypertension.
how: Usually taken once daily
Can be taken with or without food

CLOBETASOL.uses: A strong steroid cream/ointment used for severe skin conditions like eczema and psoriasis.
how: Apply a thin layer to the affected area as directed, usually once or twice daily
Use only on the area advised, for the shortest time needed
sideEffects: Thinning of skin with prolonged use
seeDoctor: Skin infection at the application site
avoid: Using on the face unless specifically told to
Covering treated skin tightly unless advised

CLOZAPINE.uses: Used for schizophrenia that hasn't responded to other treatments.
how: Taken exactly as prescribed, dose adjusted gradually by your doctor
Regular blood tests are required throughout treatment
seeDoctor: Fever, sore throat, or signs of infection (report immediately)

DAPAGLIFLOZIN.uses: A diabetes medicine that helps the kidneys remove excess sugar through urine.
how: Usually taken once daily in the morning
Can be taken with or without food
seeDoctor: Signs of a urinary or genital infection
Unusual tiredness with nausea (rare but serious)

DESLORATADINE.uses: A non-drowsy antihistamine used for allergy symptoms like sneezing, itching, and runny nose.
how: Taken once daily, with or without food

DEXAMETHASONE.uses: A steroid used to reduce inflammation and swelling in many conditions.
how: Take exactly as prescribed, usually with food
Do not stop suddenly if used for more than a few days
avoid: Live vaccines without checking with your doctor

DULOXETINE.uses: Used for depression, anxiety, and certain types of nerve pain.
how: Usually taken once daily
Swallow the capsule whole, don't crush or open it

ESCITALOPRAM.uses: Used to treat depression and anxiety disorders.
how: Usually taken once daily, with or without food
Effects may take 2-4 weeks to become noticeable

FEBUXOSTAT.uses: Lowers uric acid levels to prevent gout attacks, used when allopurinol isn't suitable.
how: Taken once daily, with or without food
Drink plenty of water
avoid: Stopping during a gout flare without medical advice

FLUCONAZOLE.uses: An antifungal medicine used for yeast infections and fungal skin/nail infections.
how: Often taken as a single dose or short course, with or without food
avoid: Taking with certain other medicines without checking

GLIMEPIRIDE.uses: Used to control blood sugar in type 2 diabetes by helping the pancreas release more insulin.
how: Usually taken once daily with breakfast or the first main meal
Don't skip meals after taking it
seeDoctor: Severe low blood sugar symptoms (confusion, fainting)

HYDROXYCHLOROQUINE.uses: Used for certain autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, and for malaria.
how: Taken with food or milk to reduce stomach upset
Effects for autoimmune conditions can take weeks to months
seeDoctor: Vision changes (regular eye check-ups are needed)

LEVOCETIRIZINE.uses: An antihistamine used for allergy symptoms such as sneezing, itching, and hives.
how: Usually taken once daily, often at night
Can be taken with or without food
avoid: Driving if it makes you drowsy

MONTELUKAST.uses: Used to prevent asthma symptoms and to relieve allergic rhinitis (hay fever).
how: Usually taken once daily in the evening
Can be taken with or without food
avoid: Using as a rescue inhaler substitute

TELMISARTAN.uses: A blood pressure medicine (ARB) that relaxes blood vessels to lower blood pressure.
how: Usually taken once daily
Can be taken with or without food
avoid: Salt substitutes high in potassium without checking with your doctor

RANITIDINE.uses: Reduces stomach acid; used for acidity, heartburn, and ulcers. Note: removed from India's NLEM in 2022 and under CDSCO monitoring for a possible cancer-linked impurity (NDMA), but it remains legally sold over the counter in India (e.g. as Aciloc, Rantac, Zinetac) as of the CDSCO's latest public statements.
how: Usually taken before meals or at bedtime, as directed
Can be taken with or without food
avoid: Self-medicating for long periods without medical review

PARACETAMOL.uses: A pain reliever and fever reducer used for headache, body ache, and fever.
how: Can be taken with or without food
Leave a gap of at least 4-6 hours between doses
avoid: Taking with other paracetamol-containing products at the same time

ONDANSETRON.uses: Prevents and treats nausea and vomiting, including after surgery or chemotherapy.
how: Usually taken as a single dose when needed, or as directed by your doctor
Tablet can be taken with or without food

METRONIDAZOLE.uses: An antibiotic used for infections caused by certain bacteria and parasites, including stomach and dental infections.
how: Usually taken with food to reduce stomach upset
Complete the full course even if you feel better
seeDoctor: No improvement after a few days
avoid: Alcohol during treatment and for 2 days after

LOPERAMIDE.uses: Controls sudden diarrhoea by slowing down gut movement.
how: Take after each loose stool, as directed
Drink plenty of fluids alongside to prevent dehydration
seeDoctor: Diarrhoea with high fever or blood in stools
avoid: Use in young children without medical advice
Using for more than 2 days without consulting a doctor

RABEPRAZOLE.uses: Reduces stomach acid; used for acidity, reflux (GERD), and ulcers.
how: Usually taken once daily before breakfast
Swallow the tablet whole, don't crush or chew

ESOMEPRAZOLE.uses: Reduces stomach acid; used for acidity, reflux (GERD), and ulcers.
how: Usually taken once daily, at least an hour before a meal
Swallow the capsule/tablet whole

DROTAVERINE.uses: Relieves spasm-related pain in the stomach, intestines, and urinary tract (e.g. period cramps, abdominal cramps).
how: Usually taken 1-3 times a day as needed, with or after food
Follow the dose your doctor recommends
seeDoctor: Pain that doesn't improve or worsens
avoid: Use without knowing the cause of the pain

MEFENAMIC ACID.uses: A pain reliever used for period pain, headache, and mild-to-moderate pain and inflammation.
how: Taken with food to reduce stomach upset
Not usually recommended for more than 7 days continuously
avoid: Use during pregnancy without medical advice

SERRATIOPEPTIDASE.uses: An enzyme medicine used to reduce swelling and inflammation, often after injury, surgery, or with infections.
how: Usually taken on an empty stomach, as directed
Often prescribed alongside another medicine for the underlying condition
avoid: Use without medical guidance for unexplained swelling

NIMESULIDE.uses: A pain and anti-inflammatory medicine used for short-term relief of pain such as joint or muscle pain.
how: Usually taken after food
Only for short-term use, as directed by a doctor

CEFPODOXIME.uses: An antibiotic used for bacterial infections of the throat, ear, sinus, and urinary tract.
how: Usually taken twice a day with food
Complete the full course even if symptoms improve
seeDoctor: No improvement after a few days

SALBUTAMOL.uses: A bronchodilator used to relieve wheezing and breathlessness in asthma and other breathing conditions.
how: Inhaler: shake well and use as directed, usually when needed
Tablet/syrup form taken as prescribed
seeDoctor: Breathlessness not relieved by the inhaler
Needing the inhaler more often than usual
avoid: Overusing the inhaler beyond prescribed frequency

LEVOSALBUTAMOL.uses: A bronchodilator used to relieve wheezing and breathlessness in asthma and other breathing conditions.
how: Inhaler: shake well and use as directed, usually when needed
Tablet/syrup form taken as prescribed
seeDoctor: Breathlessness not relieved by the inhaler
Needing the inhaler more often than usual
avoid: Overusing the inhaler beyond prescribed frequency

FERROUS SULFATE.uses: An iron supplement used to treat or prevent iron-deficiency anaemia.
how: Best absorbed on an empty stomach, but can be taken with food if it upsets your stomach
Taking with vitamin C-rich food can help absorption
seeDoctor: No improvement in fatigue after weeks of use
avoid: Taking with tea, coffee, or calcium supplements at the same time (reduces absorption)

FOLIC ACID.uses: A B-vitamin supplement used to treat or prevent folate deficiency, often prescribed during pregnancy.
how: Usually taken once daily, with or without food
avoid: Skipping doses if prescribed during pregnancy

ASCORBIC ACID.uses: Vitamin C supplement used to prevent or treat vitamin C deficiency and support wound healing.
how: Usually taken once daily, with or without food
seeDoctor: Kidney stone symptoms with long-term high-dose use
avoid: Very high doses without medical advice, especially with kidney conditions

CALCIUM CARBONATE + VITAMIN D3.uses: A supplement used to treat or prevent calcium and vitamin D deficiency, and to support bone health.
how: Usually taken once or twice daily with food
Best taken with meals to improve absorption
seeDoctor: Signs of high calcium (nausea, confusion, excessive thirst)
avoid: Taking with iron supplements at the same time (reduces absorption)

NORFLOXACIN.uses: An antibiotic mainly used for urinary tract infections and some intestinal infections.
how: Usually taken on an empty stomach, 1 hour before or 2 hours after food
Complete the full course even if you feel better
avoid: Dairy products and antacids near dosing time (reduces absorption)

OFLOXACIN.uses: An antibiotic used for urinary tract, respiratory, and some skin infections.
how: Usually taken with or without food, at evenly spaced times
Complete the full course even if you feel better
avoid: Dairy products and antacids near dosing time

TINIDAZOLE.uses: An antibiotic/antiparasitic used for infections such as giardiasis, amoebiasis, and certain bacterial infections.
how: Usually taken with food to reduce stomach upset
Often given as a short course; follow it exactly as prescribed
avoid: Alcohol during treatment and for 3 days after

NAPROXEN.uses: A pain and anti-inflammatory medicine used for joint pain, period pain, and muscle pain.
how: Taken with food or milk to reduce stomach upset
Swallow the tablet whole with water
avoid: Long-term use without a doctor's advice

TRAMADOL.uses: A prescription pain reliever used for moderate to severe pain, typically after other pain relievers haven't helped.
how: Take exactly as prescribed by your doctor, no more and no less
Can be taken with or without food
avoid: Driving or operating machinery until you know how it affects you
Using more than prescribed or for longer than advised

ITOPRIDE.uses: Helps the stomach empty faster; used for bloating, fullness, nausea, and indigestion.
how: Usually taken before meals, as directed
Follow the dosing schedule your doctor recommends
seeDoctor: Symptoms not improving after a few days

ORAL REHYDRATION SALTS.uses: Replaces water, salts, and minerals lost due to diarrhoea, vomiting, or excessive sweating, to prevent or treat dehydration.
how: Dissolve the full sachet in the exact amount of clean water stated on the pack
Sip slowly and frequently, especially after each loose stool
seeDoctor: Signs of severe dehydration (very little urine, extreme thirst, sunken eyes, lethargy)
avoid: Making the solution stronger or weaker than the instructions state
Adding sugar or salt beyond what's specified

DIGENE.uses: An antacid used for fast relief from acidity, heartburn, gas, bloating, and indigestion. The tablet/gel combines aluminium hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide, and magnesium aluminium silicate (which neutralise excess stomach acid) with simethicone (which helps break up trapped gas bubbles). One of the most widely used household antacid brands in India, made by Abbott. If you're looking this up by salt name instead of brand, search Aluminium Hydroxide + Magnesium Hydroxide + Simethicone — Gelusil is a well-known equivalent-class brand with a similar combination.
how: Tablet: chew 2-4 tablets as needed, after meals and at bedtime
Gel/liquid: take 1-2 teaspoons (5-10 ml) as needed, after meals and at bedtime
Do not exceed 4 tablets (or equivalent) in 24 hours unless a doctor says otherwise
sideEffects: Loose stools (from the magnesium component) — the two are combined partly to balance each other out
seeDoctor: Symptoms lasting more than 2 weeks despite regular use
avoid: Taking within 2 hours of other medicines — antacids can reduce absorption of many drugs (e.g. antibiotics like tetracyclines/fluoroquinolones, iron supplements, thyroid medicine)
Using daily long-term without medical advice, since it can mask a more serious underlying condition
forms: Chewable tablet (multiple flavours)
Gel/liquid (bottle)
Digene UltraFizz — effervescent powder sachet
